faq: What counts as a routine chore?

Anything repeated with clear rules, such as invoice reminders, onboarding emails, stock check messages or updating a project status. If the rules change every time, it needs a person or planning first.
Will it message my customers directly?
Only if you set it up that way. We can start with drafts for approval, then allow automatic sending of low-risk messages once you trust the wording.
Can it work across more than one tool?
Yes, within the tool count for each package. A typical case is reading a CRM, writing to a project board and messaging in Slack. We confirm each tool before we start.
What if a chore changes later?
Small changes to wording or timing are quick. For bigger changes, the Maintenance service keeps the agent matched to your tools and rules, quoted separately from this build.

desc:
Operations agents for updates and follow-ups take over the small chores that eat a team's day, such as reminders, status changes and chasing replies. Ecom Swift LLC builds the agent around your own tools, in your tone, with clear limits and a daily note of what it did.

## Where the hours go in routine operations

Most teams do not lose time on big projects. They lose it on small chores: chasing an unpaid invoice, reminding a client about a deadline, copying a status from a project board into a spreadsheet and then into an email. Each chore takes minutes, but they repeat all week and they interrupt real work.

These chores also get skipped when people are busy. A missed follow-up becomes a late payment or a client who feels ignored. A routine that runs every time, without anyone remembering, is where an agent helps most.

## What is an operations agent?

An operations agent is an automated assistant that performs recurring business tasks across your tools. It starts from a trigger, such as a schedule, a form submission or a change in a record, then reads the information it needs, takes the action and logs what it did.

Unlike a fixed automation, it can read a message, judge what it says and adjust the wording. Unlike a free-roaming assistant, it works inside rules: which chores it may do, whom it may contact, and when it must hand over to a person.

## How it changes your results

The first gain is time. Chores that took a few minutes each, several times a day, disappear from the team's list. The second gain is reliability: follow-ups go out on schedule whether or not anyone remembered.

There is also an effect on cash flow and client relationships. Invoices that are chased on day one and again later are more likely to be dealt with. Clients who receive a clear status update stop sending "any news?" messages. These are plain consequences of doing the small things consistently.

## What a good operations agent includes

- A defined list of chores, each with a trigger and an expected outcome.
- Connections to the tools you already use, such as email, a task board, a spreadsheet or a CRM.
- Message wording that matches your tone, with room for each client's details.
- Follow-up rules for what happens when there is no reply after a set time.
- Escalation to a named person when the agent is unsure or stuck.
- Approval before any message goes outside your company, when you want it.
- Different rules for different clients or teams.
- Limits on how many messages it can send in a day.
- A daily log or chat summary, plus a weekly summary of completed work.

## What we do

We begin with a list of your recurring chores and choose the ones where an agent will help most and risk least. For each one we write the steps in plain language, including the exceptions you handle by instinct, such as "never chase a client who has an open complaint".

We then build the agent in your tools, set the triggers, write the message templates in your voice and add limits and escalation. Before it goes live we run it on past examples and in a test mode that sends messages only to you. The Basic package automates one chore with a daily log. Standard handles several chores with reminders and escalation. Premium adds approvals, per-client rules, a weekly summary and a handover session for your team.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Start with chores that are repetitive, frequent and low risk.
- Write down the exceptions before the agent is built.
- Let the agent hand over to a person when a case is unclear.
- Read the daily log for the first weeks.
- Add one chore at a time once the first is stable.

**Avoid:**
- Automating a chore that your team does not yet do consistently.
- Letting the agent contact customers without a send limit.
- Using one message template for every client and situation.
- Connecting more tools than the chores need.
- Forgetting to update the rules when your process changes.

## Who this is for

This service suits a small agency that spends every Friday chasing timesheets and invoices. It suits a store team that updates order statuses in several places by hand. It also suits a manager who wants regular client updates to go out on time without writing each one.

## What we need from you

Send us a list of the chores, a few example messages in your tone and the tools involved. Give us access as a collaborator, team member or developer user in each tool, wherever the platform supports it. We never ask for passwords, and everything we build runs in your own accounts.
